F1 (the real finding). THE PR'S HEADLINE DESIGN DECISION IS UNGUARDED. D24 explicitly refused to hand-wave 'what counts as the first commit of a deliverable when a branch is merged forward', and this PR's answer is `git log --first-parent`. Deleting `--first-parent` leaves all 24 tests green (P9). I verified this is not a false alarm in both directions:
  (a) The SHIPPED CODE IS CORRECT. I built the case the flag exists for in a throwaway repo (probe kept out of the repo, in this session's scratch dir): base `main`; deliverable branch `work` with its real first commit at 09:00; a side branch off main with an EARLIER commit at 08:30; side merged into work. Plain `git log main..work --reverse` returns the SIDE commit 460c1902 first; `m.resolve_first_commit(repo,'main','work')` returns the real first commit 7a602263. `--first-parent` is load-bearing and it works.
  (b) NO TEST BUILDS THAT CASE. The one test that looks like it guards Gap 1, test_merge_forward_from_base_does_not_change_the_first_commit (tests/test_lwb_check_acceptance_criteria.py:374), merges `main` -- the BASE of the range -- forward into `work`. Everything reachable from the base is excluded by ordinary `base..head` range semantics whether or not `--first-parent` is passed, and the module docstring itself says so in as many words ('causes no confusion on that count alone... What --first-parent actually buys is protection against a genuine side branch merged WITHIN the deliverable'). So the test exercises precisely the case the code's own docstring says does not need the flag, and leaves untested the case it says does. That is the shape this repo has been bitten by before: a test written to guard a decision, that guards the one variant of it that needs no guarding.
  Not blocking, and I want to be explicit about why rather than splitting the difference: the code is right, the decision IS answered rather than hand-waved, the gate ships report-only (continue-on-error: true) so it cannot break a build, and the PR body's own mutation-probe claim is correctly SCOPED ('on the PASS/FAIL and exemption logic') -- it never claims to have probed --first-parent, so nothing here is overclaimed. The cost is future regression risk, not present incorrectness. The fix is one test: the (a) fixture above, asserting resolve_first_commit returns the real first commit. I did not write it into the PR; my authorization is record-only.
F2 (minor, same shape, lower stakes). P10: swapping `%aI` for `%cI` leaves all 24 tests green. The docstring makes a specific argument for author date ('not commit date, which a rebase can change without the author's knowledge') and nothing holds it. A rebase of a deliverable branch would silently move the anchor under the current tests. One test with a commit whose author and commit dates differ would close it.
F3 (PRE-EXISTING, NOT THIS PR'S -- and a near-miss I nearly filed against it, printed deliberately). tests/test_lwb_lanes.py::test_is_record_only_commit_true_for_a_merge_with_empty_first_parent_diff FAILS in the full-suite run on this branch. My first instinct was a regression from #68's new test module polluting it. I checked before writing it down, and was wrong three separate ways before I got it right: (i) on origin/main IN THE SAME CHECKOUT the full suite is 609/609 green, which looked like confirmation; (ii) running the new test file together with tests/test_lwb_lanes.py -> 104 passed, no failure, which killed the pollution theory; (iii) running the single test 25 times in isolation -> 23 passed, 2 FAILED. It is a genuine pre-existing FLAKE. Root cause: the test builds two commits whose ordering under `git log`'s date-ordered traversal is not deterministic when they land in the same wall-clock second, and lwb_lanes.resolve_reviewable_head on main walks `git log --format=%H <head>` with NO `--first-parent` -- so the walk descends into the side branch and can return the side commit instead of the substantive one. That is exactly the defect open PR #63 ('resolve_reviewable_head must walk first-parent history only') fixes, and #63 already carries a current AGREE record. So: #68 did not cause it, #68 must not be charged for it, and the PR body's '633 passed' is an honest report of a run where the flake did not fire. Had I not measured main and re-run in isolation I would have accused a correct PR of a regression.

There are SEVEN Outcome members (PASS, EXEMPT, FAIL, NO_ISSUE_REFERENCE, UNVERIFIABLE, NO_RANGE, CONFIG_ERROR) and FIVE distinct exit codes (0-4). The body's very next sentence describes the real 7-over-5 mapping accurately, so this is a wording slip contradicted in situ, not a claim the code fails to meet. Noted only because this repo audits quantitative claims.
F5 (low, shared-path hygiene, and one PR-body claim that is not accurate). ci.yml:195 adds `--branch ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}`. The PR body says the wiring copies lwb-proof-pr and lwb-proof-reexecute, 'both already-established mechanisms in that file; I didn't invent a third'. For --base/--head/--pr that is true. For --branch it is not: I checked every `${{ }}` interpolated into a `run:` block in ci.yml (lines 95, 126-128, 192-195, 207, 226-227, 235-237) and every pre-existing one is a sha or an integer -- character classes that cannot carry shell metacharacters. head.ref is the first FREE-TEXT, author-controlled value interpolated into a run: block in this file, and git refnames permit `;`, `&`, `|`, `$`, backtick, parentheses and quotes. That is the standard GitHub Actions script-injection shape. I am rating it LOW, honestly and deliberately: the workflow triggers on `pull_request`, whose same `test` job already executes PR-authored code (`python -m pytest -q`), so a same-repo author gains no privilege they do not already have, and fork PRs receive no secrets. It is worth noting anyway because that same `test` job does carry a real secret (LWB_PRIVATE_NEEDLES, ci.yml:81 and :92 -- I confirmed by parsing the YAML that these are the same job, not a different one). Defense-in-depth fix is one line: pass it via `env:` and reference "$BRANCH" instead of interpolating into the command.

SECOND NEAR-MISS, printed because hiding it would make this record worth less. I was about to file P11 (the trailing-'Z' rewrite in _parse_iso8601 being unguarded) as a third vacuous-guard finding. It is not one. The tests DO feed GitHub-style Z-suffixed timestamps (test file lines 119, 141, 165, 445). My probe went green only because I ran it on CPython 3.11, where datetime.fromisoformat accepts 'Z' natively. I checked both interpreters directly: python3.10 raises ValueError('Invalid isoformat string') on the same input, python3.11 accepts it. So on the 3.10 leg of this repo's own CI matrix that mutation WOULD go red, and the guard is real. The general lesson for whoever reads this next: a mutation probe run on one interpreter cannot clear a version-conditional branch, and I would have filed a false finding against a correct line of code.

WHY AGREE RATHER THAN DISAGREE. Nothing in this PR is incorrect, and nothing in it is overclaimed: I checked its quantitative claims against measurement and found one truthful-but-lucky number (F3) and one cosmetic slip in the body (F4). The mechanism works end to end against real GitHub, proven by running it on this PR itself. The distinction this repo cares about most -- 'could not check' never sharing a representation with 'checked and found nothing' -- is guarded by 8 of 8 probes. The one substantive finding (F1) is a MISSING TEST on a report-only gate, not wrong behaviour: the design decision D24 demanded is genuinely answered and correctly implemented. Blocking a correct, honestly-disclosed, non-blocking deliverable over a test that should be added costs this repository more than recording the gap does.
